title: Disinfection Verification and CT Calculations
audience: Practising drinking-water operators and supervisors seeking focused applied development.
prerequisites: Basic operator terminology, metric calculations and access to the source readings. Use a calculator; all supplied facility data are fictional.
introduction: Audit a fictional disinfection calculation, segment by segment. Reconcile effective volume, flow, residual location, timing and the conditions attached to a required CT value.
delivery: Self-paced lessons, optional quick checks, a graded final exam and a non-credit certificate. Duration is being validated; no contact-hour award is made.

modules.title: Nominal residence time and effective contact
objectives: Calculate nominal time and T10 with consistent units.
Identify evidence required to use a baffling factor.
modules.lesson: ### Start with the operating decision A CT calculation is not a way to make a number look good. It is a decision record. Before you calculate, be clear about the decision you are trying to support: can this contact segment be used for the operating condition that actually occurred? > **Your job:** show the fastest-moving water had enough supported contact time under the approved basis for your facility. That means every input must describe the same condition: the unit configuration, operating level, flow interval, residual sample point and required treatment basis. The arithmetic is easy. The operating discipline is the hard part. Do not start with a spreadsheet cell. Start with the record set. If you cannot show where a volume, flow, residual or baffling factor came from, treat the calculation as unresolved and escalate it under your plant procedure. ### Separate tank time from water time Nominal detention time is the container calculation: **T = V ÷ Q** It answers one question: at this steady flow, how long would one active tank volume take to pass through the unit? It does **not** tell you how long the fastest water travelled through it. Real clearwells and contact chambers have short paths, slower zones, inlet jetting and changes in flow pattern. Some water reaches the outlet early. That fast fraction is what matters when you are checking disinfection contact time. Think of nominal time as a first screen. It tells you whether the calculation is in the right range. It does not earn credit by itself. ### Use T10 for the fast-moving fraction **T10** is the time at which 10 percent of a tracer has reached the outlet. It represents the fast-moving fraction of the flow path. A common operational form is: **T10 = T × baffling factor** The baffling factor is not a preference and it is not a target. It is a record-supported description of the hydraulic condition. A tracer study or approved facility basis may support it for a stated configuration, water level and flow range. A factor is no longer automatically valid when a cell is isolated, a bypass is open, the water level changes outside the studied range or throughput rises beyond the tested range. In those situations, the correct question is not “what factor will pass?” It is “what basis is still supported?” ### Build the input register before using the formula Use this five-line check before you calculate: | Input | Confirm before use | |---|---| | Active volume | Operating level, compartments in service and source drawing or stage-volume record match the interval | | Flow | Correct meter, correct interval and the flow basis required by the approved procedure | | Residual | Approved sampling point and a current verification or grab check | | Baffling factor | Dated tracer study or approved basis covers this configuration and flow range | | Required CT | Correct disinfectant, temperature, pH and other conditions under the governing method | If one line fails, write the gap down. Do not fill it with an old worksheet, a laminated note or a value from memory. ### Worked method: 640 m³ at 133 L/s Use the following fictional case only to practise the method. It is not an authorized operating value. | Supplied input | Value | |---|---:| | Active chamber volume | 640 m³ | | Peak flow for the evaluated hour | 133 L/s | | Supported baffling factor | 0.30 | | Outlet free chlorine residual | 1.2 mg/L | **1. Convert flow.** 133 L/s × 3.6 = 478.8 m³/h. **2. Calculate nominal time.** 640 m³ ÷ 478.8 m³/h = 1.34 h, or 80.2 min. **3. Calculate T10.** 80.2 min × 0.30 = 24.1 min. **4. Calculate achieved CT.** 1.2 mg/L × 24.1 min = 28.9 mg·min/L. Label every line with units. That catches most errors before they become operating decisions. ### See what changes when flow rises Keep the same fictional chamber, residual and supported factor. Now increase the evaluated flow from 133 L/s to 167 L/s. The nominal time falls from 80.2 min to 63.9 min. T10 falls from 24.1 min to 19.2 min. Achieved CT falls from 28.9 to 23.0 mg·min/L. The important lesson is not the exact number. It is the direction of the risk. When flow rises, contact time falls. A higher flow can also change the residence-time pattern, which means the earlier baffling factor may no longer be supported. > **Operating implication:** a calculation that was acceptable at one flow is not automatically valid at a higher flow. Check the tested range before carrying the factor forward. ### Estimate before you calculate Before you use the calculator, estimate the answer. A 640 m3 chamber at 480 m3/h turns over in about 1.3 hours, so a nominal time near three hours at that flow points to a unit or flow error. Estimating first catches most conversion slips, and it tells you whether a result is worth checking further. ### Know the stop conditions Stop and resolve the record before relying on the result when any of these conditions apply: - A compartment is isolated, bypassed or returned to service. - The operating level is outside the range used for the volume or tracer basis. - The flow is outside the supported range. - The residual came from a different point or time than the evaluated interval. - A posted factor has no dated source, conditions or approval reference. - The required CT lookup does not match the actual disinfectant, temperature or pH. A calculation can be numerically correct and still be operationally unusable. Mark it as a sensitivity check if it helps planning, but do not represent it as a supported determination. ### Common errors **Reading a nameplate volume as the active volume.** A tank's structural volume includes freeboard and dead space that the tracer study may have excluded. Use the level-to-volume value for the level you actually recorded, not the figure on the drawing. **Dividing by a flow from the wrong interval.** A daily average flow is smaller than the peak hour, so nominal time comes out too long. The result can look comfortable and still describe a condition that did not occur at the peak. **Using a worked example as a template.** The 640 m3 chamber and the 133 L/s case in this lesson are teaching values. Re-run the method on the record for your own interval. Never reuse a result from a different interval. **Carrying a factor past the configuration it was measured for.** A factor measured with two cells in service says nothing about one cell. Record which cells, which level band and which flow range the factor covers, and treat the factor as unsupported outside them. ### Finish the shift with a defensible record Before you sign the calculation, record the unit configuration, operating level, flow interval, residual sample point, temperature, pH, baffling-factor source and required-CT basis. Attach or reference the underlying trend, calibration check and tracer or approval record. For Ontario facilities, the applicable disinfection procedure and your facility approvals set the basis you may use. Your operating manual tells you what to do when the basis is not available. General guidance can help you understand the method, but it cannot replace the documents that govern your works. If records conflict, use the most conservative supported basis, document the conflict and notify the designated responsible person under your procedure.

### Fictional scenario: Clearwell 2 during valve repair

Maplecrest Water Treatment Plant is checking contact time from 14:00 to 15:00. The historian shows a peak flow of 152 L/s. The level record shows 3.10 m. A stage-volume curve gives 860 m³ active volume with **both** clearwell cells in service. Outlet free chlorine is 0.95 mg/L and the analyzer was grab-checked that morning.

Three records conflict:

1. A laminated card says “Clearwell 2 baffling factor 0.70” with no date, author or source.
2. A tracer report from two years earlier supports a factor of 0.42, but only with both cells in service at 3.10 m and 400 to 620 m³/h.
3. The shift log says Cell B was isolated for valve repair at 13:40.

### Your decision

Reject the laminated card. It has no evidence behind it. Do not use 860 m³ or 0.42 as a creditable basis either, because both records describe two-cell service and Cell B is isolated.

You may calculate the two-cell condition as a **sensitivity check** to understand the exposure, but you cannot claim it as the operating determination. Record the conflict, move to the conservative supported single-cell basis in the approved procedure, notify the responsible operator and request a hydraulic verification for the single-cell configuration.
modules.assignment: Using the Clearwell 2 record for 14:00 to 15:00, build an input register and calculation audit. Convert the 152 L/s peak flow to m3/h, then calculate nominal time and T10 for the two-cell tracer basis (860 m3 with a factor of 0.42). Compare that basis with the undated laminated card's factor of 0.70. Calculate achieved CT at 0.95 mg/L and label it a conditional sensitivity, not a determination. List the evidence needed to approve a single-cell hydraulic basis. The record does not contain a single-cell volume, so do not calculate one.
rubric: Converts 152 L/s to 547.2 m3/h and gets 94.3 min nominal time and 39.6 min T10 for the two-cell basis.
Distinguishes the 0.42 factor, valid only for two cells at 3.10 m and 400 to 620 m3/h, from the undated 0.70 card.
Labels the 37.6 mg.min/L result as a conditional sensitivity, not a CT determination.
modules.facilitatorGuide: Two-cell nominal time is 860 m3 divided by 547.2 m3/h, which is 94.3 min. T10 at the tracer factor 0.42 is 39.6 min. The laminated card's 0.70 would give 66.0 min, but it has no date, author or source, so it is rejected. The sensitivity CT is 0.95 mg/L times 39.6 min, which is 37.6 mg.min/L. It is not an authorized determination because Cell B was isolated at 13:40. Require learners to name the 3.10 m level and the 400 to 620 m3/h range that the tracer covers. Do not accept a factor chosen to make the result pass, and do not accept a single-cell CT, because the record gives no single-cell volume.

checks.prompt: Nominal detention time, calculated as T equals V divided by Q, tells the operator which of the following about a contact chamber?
choices: The time needed to displace one basin volume at that steady flow
Time the fastest ten percent of the water spends in the unit
Travel time along the shortest inlet to outlet path in the unit
Time for the disinfectant residual to decay across the chamber
checks.explanation: Nominal time is V divided by Q: the time to displace one basin volume at a steady flow. The fastest-ten-percent choice describes T10 from a tracer curve, not V divided by Q. The shortest-path choice describes a flow path, and the decay choice describes the residual, which V divided by Q does not measure.

checks.prompt: A SCADA tag reports flow through a fictional clearwell as 145 L/s. For a T equals V over Q calculation in cubic metres per hour, this flow converts to:
checks.explanation: 1 L/s equals 3.6 m3/h, so 145 L/s is 522 m3/h. The 60.4 choice divides by 2.4 instead of multiplying by 3.6. The 8.7 choice is 145 L/s in m3/min, mislabelled as m3/h. The 12,528 choice multiplies by 86.4, which converts to cubic metres per day, not per hour.

checks.prompt: A fictional tracer study reports T10 equal to 30 min while nominal time at the test condition is 100 min. The baffling factor for that tested condition is:
choices: 30 min
checks.explanation: BF is T10 divided by T: 30 divided by 100 gives 0.30, a dimensionless ratio. The 3.33 choice inverts the ratio (T over T10). The 30 min choice is T10 itself, which carries time units and cannot be a factor. The 0.70 choice is the fraction of the test water not yet through at T10, not the factor.

checks.prompt: Which single item, on its own, is acceptable evidence supporting the baffling factor used in a CT calculation at an Ontario drinking water facility?
choices: A laminated card posted beside the chlorine analyzer panel
A verbal value passed on by the previous shift operator
A spreadsheet cell holding the number with no source noted
A dated tracer study report with test flow, level and curve
checks.explanation: A factor needs a dated, reproducible source: a tracer study or the value in the approved manual or approval. The laminated card has no test conditions, validity range or date. The verbal value from the previous shift and the spreadsheet cell with no source note are both unsourced, so neither can support the number.

checks.prompt: A fictional contact chamber holds an active volume of 550 m3 and steady flow through it is 250 m3/h. What is the nominal detention time?
choices: 132 minutes
220 minutes
0.45 hours
27 minutes
checks.explanation: 550 divided by 250 is 2.2 h, and 2.2 times 60 is 132 min. The 220 minute choice divides by 2.5 instead of 250, a misplaced decimal in the flow. The 0.45 hours choice inverts the ratio to Q over V. The 27 minute choice is that inverted 0.45 hours converted to minutes.

checks.prompt: When verifying contact time for a specific evaluated interval, the governing method normally directs the operator to base T on which flow value?
choices: Lowest recorded flow through the unit during the interval
Peak flow through the unit during that evaluated interval
Daily average flow taken from the historian for that day
Nameplate design capacity listed for the contact chamber
checks.explanation: Contact time must reflect the fast-moving fraction, so the peak flow in the evaluated interval is normally the basis. The lowest-flow choice gives the longest nominal time and overstates T10 at the peak. The daily average smooths out the peak hour and overstates T10. The nameplate design capacity is a design figure, not the flow in that interval.

modules.title: Residual, required CT and calculation boundaries
objectives: Calculate achieved CT and a comparison ratio.
Match residual and required CT to the correct conditions.
modules.lesson:
### What the CT number actually represents

CT is a single number that stands in for a larger claim. Writing 28.0 mg·min/L asserts that a defined parcel of water, moving through a defined piece of equipment under defined chemistry, received a defined residual for a defined minimum time. If any boundary is wrong, the arithmetic is still right and the conclusion is worthless.

The basic form is achieved CT = C × T. C is the residual that the governing method says represents the segment, and T is the supported contact time in minutes, conventionally T10. The Procedure for Disinfection of Drinking Water in Ontario sets the CT concept, the T10 basis and the disinfectant-specific requirements, so it decides what counts as an acceptable C and T at your works.

The comparison ratio is achieved CT divided by the applicable required CT. A ratio of 1.00 means equality. It does not mean the water was safe or the record is defensible. Report every CT with its segment, flow, residual point, temperature, pH and the source of the required value.

### Fixing C: the residual that belongs to the segment

Three distinctions matter every time. Species: free and total chlorine are different measurements, and required CT is disinfectant specific, so a total reading used against a free requirement overstates credit. Location: the governing method fixes the representative sample point, most commonly the segment outlet. An inlet or mid-chamber reading is not a substitute because it is higher. Time: the residual must represent the evaluated interval, and analyzer data count only when the measurement chain is sound (sample line lag, calibration, drift and grab verification; compare EPA 815-B-19-010, a US technical guide, not Ontario law). When instrument and grab disagree beyond procedure tolerance, suspend the calculation. Do not average them or pick the higher.

### Fixing T: volume, flow and the supported T10

T10 is not a nameplate figure or theoretical detention time. Use the effective volume at the operating level, the peak flow for the evaluated interval (a daily average hides the peak), and a supported baffling basis. A factor lapses when the configuration changes: a removed baffle, an isolated chamber, an open bypass or a level outside the tracer's range. A T10 validated for two chambers in series is not valid for one.

### Worked example 1: single segment achieved CT and comparison ratio

All values below are supplied case assumptions for this teaching example at a fictional plant. They are not authorized values for any real works.

Supplied: contact chamber effective volume 640 m³; peak hourly flow through the segment 118 L/s; approved baffling factor 0.50 from the tracer basis on file; free chlorine at the approved segment outlet point 0.62 mg/L; required CT for the example conditions assumed to be 22 mg·min/L.

Step 1, convert flow to consistent units.
Q = 118 L/s × 60 s/min = 7 080 L/min
Q = 7 080 L/min ÷ 1 000 L/m³ = 7.080 m³/min

Step 2, theoretical detention time.
TDT = 640 m³ ÷ 7.080 m³/min = 90.40 min

Step 3, supported contact time.
T10 = 90.40 min × 0.50 = 45.20 min

Step 4, achieved CT.
CT achieved = 0.62 mg/L × 45.20 min = 28.02 mg·min/L

Step 5, comparison ratio.
Ratio = 28.02 mg·min/L ÷ 22 mg·min/L = 1.27

Answer: achieved CT is 28.0 mg·min/L and the comparison ratio is 1.27 against the supplied required value, valid only if the residual point, the baffling basis, the flow figure and the required-value conditions all hold.

Now change one condition. Suppose the same interval is re-evaluated at a peak flow of 145 L/s.
Q = 145 L/s × 60 s/min = 8 700 L/min = 8.700 m³/min
TDT = 640 m³ ÷ 8.700 m³/min = 73.56 min
T10 = 73.56 min × 0.50 = 36.78 min
CT achieved = 0.62 mg/L × 36.78 min = 22.80 mg·min/L
Ratio = 22.80 mg·min/L ÷ 22 mg·min/L = 1.04

A 23 percent flow increase consumed almost all of the margin. That is the number's real message: CT margin is mostly a hydraulic statement, and it moves with flow much faster than most operators expect.

### Matching required CT to the actual conditions

Required CT is condition specific. Spellman's handbook says the required value "will vary depending on pH, temperature, and the organisms to be killed". It does not tie the requirement to the residual concentration, and this course follows that wording. Check the governing lookup before you use any table, because a textbook table is a teaching source and not your facility's authority.

The table used here is Spellman's Table 18.15. It gives 104 mg.min/L as the CT for 3-log inactivation of Giardia cysts by chlorine at 10 °C. The handbook states that its Giardia values assume 10 °C and a pH from 6 to 9, and that chlorine becomes less effective as pH rises across that range. The table has no value at other temperatures, so a reading at any other temperature needs a lookup from the method that governs your works.

**Worked example 2.** Supplied case assumptions: free chlorine residual at the approved point 0.80 mg/L; supported T10 for the segment 100 min; measured temperature 10 °C; measured pH 7.6.

Step 1, achieved CT.
CT achieved = 0.80 mg/L × 100 min = 80.0 mg.min/L

Step 2, required CT. The measured conditions match Table 18.15: 10 °C, pH 7.6 within the 6 to 9 band, 3-log Giardia, chlorine. Required CT = 104 mg.min/L. The table gives one value for this band, so no interpolation is applied.

Step 3, comparison ratio.
Ratio = 80.0 mg.min/L ÷ 104 mg.min/L = 0.77

Answer: the ratio is 0.77, so the comparison is not met for these supplied conditions.

Step 4, the residual target. The residual that would give a ratio of 1.00 at this T10 is 104 mg.min/L ÷ 100 min = 1.04 mg/L. One division is enough here because the handbook ties the required value to pH, temperature and organism, not to the residual. The target is still a number to check against the residual limits in your approval and procedure. It is not a residual the plant has achieved.

The trap is to treat 1.04 mg/L as a result. It holds only while the temperature and pH stay within the conditions above. A colder interval, or a pH outside the 6 to 9 band, requires a new lookup before any target is used.

### The input register and validity screen

Use a register like this before you compute anything. If a row fails, the calculation does not proceed.

| Input | Where it comes from | Acceptance check | Invalidates the calculation if | Record retained |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Organism and log credit claimed | Facility approval and governing procedure | Matches the credit the works is relying on | Credit assumed rather than established | Approval extract, basis memo |
| Disinfectant and species | Approved basis and analyzer configuration | Free versus total matches the required-CT basis | Total reading used against a free basis | Analyzer configuration record |
| Residual value | Approved sample point, analyzer or grab | Within calibration tolerance, grab verification current | Overdue verification, stale sample line, wrong point | Calibration and verification logs |
| Temperature | Approved measurement point and interval | Represents the evaluated interval | Daily average used to mask a cold period | Continuous trend or logged reading |
| pH | Approved measurement point | Within the tabulated band or handled by the prescribed rule | pH outside table range with no prescribed rule | Instrument log, calibration record |
| Flow through the segment | Metered flow for the evaluated interval | Peak basis as prescribed, meter verification current | Daily average substituted for peak | SCADA trend, meter verification |
| Effective segment volume | Approved basis and operating level | Level-corrected where the method requires | Full structural volume used on a drawn-down tank | Level trend, volume table |
| T10 basis | Tracer study or approved baffling factor | Configuration matches the validated configuration | Chamber out of service, bypass open, baffle altered | Tracer report, configuration log |
| Required CT | Governing procedure and approved basis | All conditions matched, interpolation rule stated | Row selected for conditions other than the measured ones | Lookup printout with conditions noted |
| Ratio and conclusion | Calculation sheet | Computed at full precision, rounded once at the end | Intermediate rounding used to cross 1.00 | Signed calculation record |

Records are not optional housekeeping. O. Reg. 128/04 addresses the designation of overall responsible operators and operators in charge, their duties and record requirements at sections 23 and 25 to 27, and a CT determination is an operational decision that a designated person owns. The name attached to the calculation matters as much as the number.

### Common errors

**Using the inlet or a mid-chamber residual because it is higher.** This inflates C and CT directly. Compare the recorded value with the approved sample point.

**Treating theoretical detention time as T10.** Volume divided by flow overstates T by about 3.3 times at a factor of 0.3.

**Averaging the flow across the interval.** Peak flow sets the shortest contact time, and an average removes it.

**Rounding intermediate steps until a ratio crosses 1.00.** Round once, at the end, and record the unrounded ratio.

### What to verify before you act

Before you rely on a CT result, check the documents, not memory: the Ontario disinfection procedure for the CT concept and T10; the works permit and licence for the credited configuration and sample points; the tracer study or baffling determination for that configuration; calibration records for the analyzer, pH, temperature and flow instruments; and your procedure for ratios below 1.00 or failed input checks, including who is notified. O. Reg. 128/04, sections 23 and 25 to 27, sets designation, duties and records. A required value that is not established for the measured conditions is an unresolved determination, escalated under your procedure.

### Fictional worked scenario

**All facilities, operators, records and readings below are fictional and are supplied only as case assumptions for this exercise. No value here is an authorized figure for any real works.**

Maple Hollow Water Treatment Plant, fictional. Operator M. Devereaux is verifying CT for the post-filter contact chamber for the 07:00 to 08:00 interval on a fictional date.

Supplied values:
- Effective chamber volume at operating level: 410 m³
- Peak flow through the segment during the interval: 96 L/s
- Baffling factor from the tracer study on file: 0.30
- Free chlorine at the approved segment outlet point: 0.71 mg/L
- Temperature: 14.6 °C, pH: 7.9
- Required CT for these example conditions, supplied assumption: 48 mg·min/L

Records in the shift log that must be rejected:
1. A handwritten entry reading "T10 = 70 min (design nameplate)." This is close to volume divided by flow and ignores the 0.30 baffling factor. It is not a supported T10 and the tracer report on file is the governing basis.
2. A note reading "use inlet residual 1.12 mg/L, better signal." The approved representative point for this segment is the outlet. The inlet value is real but not applicable.

Worked solution:

Q = 96 L/s × 60 s/min = 5 760 L/min
Q = 5 760 L/min ÷ 1 000 L/m³ = 5.760 m³/min
TDT = 410 m³ ÷ 5.760 m³/min = 71.18 min
T10 = 71.18 min × 0.30 = 21.35 min
CT achieved = 0.71 mg/L × 21.35 min = 15.16 mg·min/L
Ratio = 15.16 mg·min/L ÷ 48 mg·min/L = 0.32

What the rejected records would have produced:
CT = 1.12 mg/L × 70 min = 78.4 mg·min/L
Ratio = 78.4 mg·min/L ÷ 48 mg·min/L = 1.63

The two unsupported inputs would have turned a ratio of 0.32 into an apparent 1.63, a fivefold error. Correct outcome: record the ratio of 0.32, flag the interval, notify the overall responsible operator, retain the tracer report, the analyzer calibration record and the SCADA flow trend, and follow the plant's authorized response procedure. Do not amend the log to fit the favourable numbers.
modules.assignment: Using the Maple Hollow post-filter record for 07:00 to 08:00, calculate the valid achieved CT and comparison ratio, compare the result with the rejected worksheet, and write an action and uncertainty note. Explain which inputs must be re-verified before the next interval, and why an unchanged 0.71 mg/L residual does not establish an unchanged required CT. Include units and the limits of the supplied requirement of 48 mg.min/L.
rubric: Calculates achieved CT 15.2 mg.min/L and ratio 0.32 from 410 m3, 96 L/s, factor 0.30 and 0.71 mg/L.
Rejects the 1.12 mg/L inlet residual and the 70 min nameplate T10.
Does not invent a cold-water requirement or claim compliance.
modules.facilitatorGuide: Nominal time is 410 m3 divided by 5.76 m3/min, which is 71.2 min. T10 is 71.2 min times 0.30, which is 21.4 min. CT is 0.71 mg/L times 21.35 min, which is 15.2 mg.min/L, and the ratio is 15.2 divided by 48, which is 0.32. The two rejected entries, a 70 min nameplate T10 and the 1.12 mg/L inlet residual, give 78.4 mg.min/L and a ratio of 1.63, about five times the supported result. At 14.6 °C and pH 7.9, the requirement must be looked up again for those conditions; do not carry the supplied 48 forward to another interval. Require the authorized response and escalation, not an unapproved dose change. Extra decimal places cannot repair an input mismatch.

checks.prompt: Achieved CT is the product of a disinfectant residual in mg/L and a supported contact time in minutes. What units does that product carry?
choices: L·min/mg
mg·h/L
mg·min/L
mg/L·s
checks.explanation: C in mg/L multiplied by T in minutes gives mg.min/L. Writing it as mg.h/L shrinks the number by 60 and does not match published tables. L.min/mg is the inverse combination of units, and mg/L.s mixes a seconds unit into a minutes product. None of the three is the CT unit.

checks.prompt: In CT verification, what does T10 represent for a contact segment?
choices: The time needed to fill the segment from empty to overflow level
The segment volume divided by flow with no reduction applied
The time in which 90 percent of a tracer input has passed the outlet
The time in which 10 percent of a tracer input has passed the outlet
checks.explanation: T10 is the time in which 10 percent of a tracer input reaches the outlet, which protects the fastest-moving water. The fill-time choice describes filling, not contact. The 90 percent choice describes the bulk of the flow, the wrong end of the curve. Volume divided by flow with no reduction is theoretical detention time, which overstates the contact actually supported.

checks.prompt: Your approved basis names a specific residual sample point for a contact segment. Which reading should be used as C for that segment?
choices: The residual measured at the sample point the governing method specifies
The arithmetic mean of the inlet and mid-chamber residual readings
The highest residual found anywhere along the chamber that shift
The residual measured at the segment inlet, since dosing occurs there
checks.explanation: The governing method fixes the representative residual point, commonly the outlet. The highest residual anywhere in the chamber is chosen to improve the ratio. The mean of inlet and mid-chamber readings mixes points that do not represent the water at the segment end. The inlet reading is real but is not the point the approved basis uses.

checks.prompt: Teaching example with supplied case assumptions at a fictional plant: segment effective volume 300 m³, flow through the segment 50 L/s, approved baffling factor 0.60. What is the supported T10 in minutes?
choices: 100 min
60 min
167 min
36 min
checks.explanation: 50 L/s is 3.0 m3/min; 300 divided by 3.0 gives 100 min of theoretical detention time, and 100 times 0.60 gives 60 min. The 100 min choice omits the baffling factor. The 36 min choice applies the factor twice (60 times 0.60). The 167 min choice divides 100 by 0.60, which inflates contact time instead of reducing it.

checks.prompt: A verification sheet shows a comparison ratio of 1.45, but the T10 used came from a baffling basis that was never validated for the present configuration. How should this determination be characterised?
choices: A passing determination, provided the residual reading was in tolerance
A passing determination, because the margin above 1.00 is comfortable
An unresolved determination, because validity is judged separately from the ratio
An acceptable determination once the ratio is rounded down to 1.40
checks.explanation: The ratio and the validity assessment are separate outputs, so an invalid T10 leaves the determination unresolved whatever the margin. The comfortable-margin choice treats 1.45 as a result despite the invalid basis. The residual-in-tolerance choice checks only the residual, not the hydraulic basis. Rounding 1.45 down to 1.40 changes the number and still leaves the basis unsupported.

checks.prompt: A continuous chlorine analyzer and a verification grab sample disagree by more than the tolerance stated in your procedure. What is the correct handling for the CT calculation?
choices: Use the lower of the two readings and note the difference on the sheet
Use the higher of the two readings because it is the safer record
Average the analyzer value and the grab value and use the mean as C
Suspend the calculation until the discrepancy is investigated and resolved
checks.explanation: A disagreement beyond tolerance means the true residual is not known, so the calculation is suspended until it is resolved. Using the lower reading understates CT and is a choice of convenience. Averaging produces a number that neither instrument supports. Using the higher reading selects a value because it looks safer, which is the same error as choosing the favourable result.

modules.title: Segment calculations and time alignment
objectives: Combine segment ratios only under an explicitly allowed method.
modules.lesson:
### What a segment actually is

A segment is a stretch of the disinfection train where one residual and one residence time can honestly describe the water. It starts at a disinfectant application or residual measurement and ends at the next measurement or change in hydraulic character. The method referenced in your approval decides which segments you may recognise and how their results combine, not operator preference or a SCADA screen. Redrawing a boundary mid-shift to capture more volume is a modelling change, and it needs authority.

All facilities and readings here are fictional.

### Why segments cannot simply be added

Two failures recur: adding contact times and multiplying by the best residual, and adding achieved CT values to compare with one requirement. Each segment can have its own temperature, pH, residual and required CT. Where the method permits combination, the usual form is ratio summation: each segment is evaluated against its own requirement and the dimensionless ratios are added. The lesson uses a supplied fictional rule (a sum of at least 1.0). It is a teaching device only.

### Worked example 1: two segments in series

Fictional Plant A, supplied case assumptions. Segment A is a baffled contact tank with an effective volume of 450 m3 and a supplied validated baffling factor of 0.5. Segment B is a transmission main to the first user with a credited volume of 210 m3 and a supplied baffling factor of 0.9. Instantaneous plant flow at the interval of interest is 6,800 m3/d. The residual measured at the outlet of segment A is 0.55 mg/L. The residual measured at the end of segment B is 0.42 mg/L. The supplied required CT values for the stated temperature, pH and residual conditions are 36 mg.min/L for segment A and 38 mg.min/L for segment B.

Step 1, convert flow to volumetric units that match the tank volume.
- Q = 6,800 m3/d divided by 1,440 min/d = 4.722 m3/min

Step 2, theoretical detention time in segment A.
- TDT(A) = 450 m3 divided by 4.722 m3/min = 95.30 min

Step 3, contact time credited in segment A.
- T10(A) = 95.30 min multiplied by 0.5 = 47.65 min

Step 4, achieved CT in segment A.
- CT(A) = 0.55 mg/L multiplied by 47.65 min = 26.21 mg.min/L

Step 5, inactivation ratio for segment A.
- R(A) = 26.21 mg.min/L divided by 36 mg.min/L = 0.73

Step 6, theoretical detention time in segment B at the same flow.
- TDT(B) = 210 m3 divided by 4.722 m3/min = 44.47 min

Step 7, contact time credited in segment B.
- T10(B) = 44.47 min multiplied by 0.9 = 40.02 min

Step 8, achieved CT in segment B.
- CT(B) = 0.42 mg/L multiplied by 40.02 min = 16.81 mg.min/L

Step 9, inactivation ratio for segment B.
- R(B) = 16.81 mg.min/L divided by 38 mg.min/L = 0.44

Step 10, sum the ratios under the supplied rule.
- Sum = 0.73 plus 0.44 = 1.17

Answer: the supplied ratio sum is 1.17, which meets the supplied acceptance value of 1.0 for this fictional example.

Now the shortcut that operators reach for. Take the higher residual across the total credited time.
- T total = 47.65 min plus 40.02 min = 87.67 min
- CT shortcut = 0.55 mg/L multiplied by 87.67 min = 48.22 mg.min/L
- Ratio shortcut = 48.22 mg.min/L divided by 36 mg.min/L = 1.34

The shortcut reports 1.34 against a true supplied value of 1.17. It applies a residual to water that never carried it and compares the total against a denominator that only applied to segment A. In a marginal case, the same error converts a fail into a pass.

### Time alignment: inputs must have coexisted

A CT result describes one moment. Every input must come from the same interval, normally the worst-case interval the method requires. The failure is quiet: a worksheet pairs the morning's best residual with the afternoon's lowest flow.

Fictional Plant A, supplied fifteen-minute SCADA record for one morning.

| Time | Flow (m3/d) | Residual at A outlet (mg/L) | Residual at B end (mg/L) | Temp (C) | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 06:00 | 5,200 | 0.62 | 0.49 | 14 | steady |
| 06:15 | 5,400 | 0.62 | 0.48 | 14 | steady |
| 06:30 | 8,900 | 0.58 | 0.44 | 14 | pumps stepping up |
| 06:45 | 11,400 | no data | 0.33 | 13 | analyzer in calibration |
| 07:00 | 11,600 | 0.41 | 0.30 | 13 | peak |

Supplied required CT values at 13 C for this example are 44 mg.min/L for segment A and 46 mg.min/L for segment B.

### Worked example 2: the aligned interval against the mismatched one

Aligned calculation at 07:00, using only 07:00 inputs.
- Q = 11,600 m3/d divided by 1,440 min/d = 8.056 m3/min
- TDT(A) = 450 m3 divided by 8.056 m3/min = 55.86 min
- T10(A) = 55.86 min multiplied by 0.5 = 27.93 min
- CT(A) = 0.41 mg/L multiplied by 27.93 min = 11.45 mg.min/L
- R(A) = 11.45 mg.min/L divided by 44 mg.min/L = 0.26
- TDT(B) = 210 m3 divided by 8.056 m3/min = 26.07 min
- T10(B) = 26.07 min multiplied by 0.9 = 23.46 min
- CT(B) = 0.30 mg/L multiplied by 23.46 min = 7.04 mg.min/L
- R(B) = 7.04 mg.min/L divided by 46 mg.min/L = 0.15
- Sum = 0.26 plus 0.15 = 0.41

Answer: the aligned supplied ratio sum at 07:00 is 0.41, well short of the supplied acceptance value of 1.0.

Mismatched calculation, the one that appears on a careless sheet. It uses the daily average flow of 6,900 m3/d with the best residuals of the morning, recorded at 06:15.
- Q = 6,900 m3/d divided by 1,440 min/d = 4.792 m3/min
- TDT(A) = 450 m3 divided by 4.792 m3/min = 93.91 min
- T10(A) = 93.91 min multiplied by 0.5 = 46.96 min
- CT(A) = 0.62 mg/L multiplied by 46.96 min = 29.11 mg.min/L
- R(A) = 29.11 mg.min/L divided by 44 mg.min/L = 0.66
- TDT(B) = 210 m3 divided by 4.792 m3/min = 43.82 min
- T10(B) = 43.82 min multiplied by 0.9 = 39.44 min
- CT(B) = 0.48 mg/L multiplied by 39.44 min = 18.93 mg.min/L
- R(B) = 18.93 mg.min/L divided by 46 mg.min/L = 0.41
- Sum = 0.66 plus 0.41 = 1.07

Answer: the mismatched supplied ratio sum is 1.07, an apparent pass built from inputs that were forty-five minutes apart and from a flow that no pump was producing during the peak. The difference between 0.41 and 1.07 is mainly an alignment artifact.

The 06:45 gap is a second judgment point: a trend line across it is a drawing, not a measurement. Handle it under the approved gap rule and keep it visible. The US EPA turbidity guidance (EPA 815-B-19-010) is background only: it is US technical guidance, not Ontario law.

### Input register and decision table

Inputs must declare timestamp and validity first.

| Input | Source and tag | Timestamp | Value and units | Validity check | Retained record |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Plant flow | FIT-101 instantaneous | 07:00 | 11,600 m3/d | within calibration, no alarm | SCADA historian export |
| Segment A volume | approved method, tank 1 | static | 450 m3 | matches approved basis | approval document extract |
| Segment A baffling factor | validated basis | static | 0.5 | configuration matches validation | tracer or approval record |
| Segment A residual | AIT-210 | 07:00 | 0.41 mg/L | verified against grab sample | bench sheet plus historian |
| Segment B residual | AIT-240 | 07:00 | 0.30 mg/L | last calibration in date | bench sheet plus historian |
| Temperature | TIT-205 | 07:00 | 13 C | plausible versus seasonal trend | historian |
| Required CT, each segment | approved lookup | 07:00 conditions | 44 and 46 mg.min/L | correct table, correct conditions | printed lookup page, initialled |

| Situation | Permitted action under an authorized ratio method | Not permitted |
|---|---|---|
| Two segments in series, both measured | Evaluate each against its own required CT, sum the ratios | Add the contact times and use one residual |
| Two parallel paths | Assess each path separately on its own hydraulics | Treat the paths as consecutive segments |
| Residual gap in one interval | Apply the approved gap rule, flag the interval | Interpolate and present the result as measured |
| Configuration changed, for example a bypass opened | Recalculate using the baffling basis for that configuration | Reuse the validated factor from the normal configuration |
| Mixed timestamps available | Use the worst aligned interval the method requires | Pair the best residual with the lowest flow |

### Common errors

**Borrowing a residual across a segment boundary.** Applying the segment A outlet residual to the whole train assumes no demand or decay downstream. Example 1 shows the inflation.

**Averaging the flow to soften a peak.** Contact time varies inversely with flow, so the peak interval normally controls. Example 2 shows the difference.

**Promoting a baffling factor without authority.** Writing 1.0 because a tank looks like plug flow discards the validated basis.

**Reading the wrong table row.** Required CT moves with temperature, pH and disinfectant, so a warm-weather row or a free-chlorine row on a chloramine plant changes every ratio.

**Presenting an interpolated gap as data.** A filled value must be labelled as a substitution under the approved rule.

### What to verify before you act

Before you combine anything, confirm the governing method, that a segment combination method is explicitly allowed, and its acceptance basis and pathogen target. Confirm segment definitions, credited volumes and baffling factors against the approval or validation record, and confirm the plant is in the configuration those factors describe. O. Reg. 128/04 sets operator designation and records duties. Retain the historian export, bench sheets, calibration records and initialled lookup page. A calculation you cannot reconstruct from retained inputs is not verification.
modules.evidence:
### Fictional worked scenario: Kettle Bay Water Treatment Plant

All facility details, operators, records and readings below are fictional and are supplied only as teaching assumptions. They are not authorized values.

Supplied facts. Kettle Bay operates free chlorine primary disinfection. Segment A is a clearwell with a credited volume of 380 m3 and a validated baffling factor of 0.3. Segment B is the main to the first user with a credited volume of 165 m3 and a baffling factor of 0.9. The facility method, for this exercise only, permits ratio summation across the two segments with an acceptance sum of 1.0. At the 09:45 peak interval the historian shows flow 9,400 m3/d, residual at the segment A outlet 0.71 mg/L, residual at the end of segment B 0.58 mg/L, and water temperature 9 C. Supplied required CT values for these conditions are 38 mg.min/L for segment A and 40 mg.min/L for segment B.

Records to reject. The daily CT sheet signed by a fictional operator shows "Segment A T10 = 58 min" with a margin note "clearwell is plug flow, BF 1.0". No tracer study, validation record or approval text supports a factor of 1.0, so that entry is unsupported and must be rejected. The same sheet uses a residual of 0.94 mg/L recorded at 06:10 for the 09:45 interval. That value is noncontemporaneous and must also be rejected.

Correct calculation.
- Q = 9,400 m3/d divided by 1,440 min/d = 6.528 m3/min
- TDT(A) = 380 m3 divided by 6.528 m3/min = 58.21 min
- T10(A) = 58.21 min multiplied by 0.3 = 17.46 min
- CT(A) = 0.71 mg/L multiplied by 17.46 min = 12.40 mg.min/L
- R(A) = 12.40 divided by 38 = 0.33
- TDT(B) = 165 m3 divided by 6.528 m3/min = 25.28 min
- T10(B) = 25.28 min multiplied by 0.9 = 22.75 min
- CT(B) = 0.58 mg/L multiplied by 22.75 min = 13.20 mg.min/L
- R(B) = 13.20 divided by 40 = 0.33
- Sum = 0.66

The rejected sheet produced 58.21 min multiplied by 0.94 mg/L = 54.72 mg.min/L, divided by 38 = 1.44, plus 0.33 for segment B, for a claimed sum of 1.77. Answer: the defensible supplied result is 0.66, a failed interval. Flag it, follow the facility procedure for a disinfection shortfall, and retain the historian export, the rejected sheet and the validation record for the 0.3 factor.

Name one prohibited shortcut and its numerical consequence.

The sum is 0.66, below the supplied acceptance value of 1.0, so the interval is a failure to flag and escalate. The rejected sheet uses factor 1.0 (T10 58 min) and a 06:10 residual of 0.94 mg/L.
